key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: Before a State may sever the rights of parents in their natural child, due process requires that it support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence; a fair preponderance standard is unconstitutional in a permanent neglect proceeding.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling federal authority behind Ohio's clear-and-convincing requirement in R.C. 2151.414.
key_cases.quote: Evaluation of the three Eldridge factors compels the conclusion that use of a "fair preponderance of the evidence" standard in such proceedings is inconsistent with due process.

key_cases.holding: A juvenile court may not find that a child cannot or should not be placed with either parent unless it finds by clear and convincing evidence that at least one of the then eight enumerated R.C. 2151.414(E) factors exists; general concerns outside the list will not do.
key_cases.relevance: This is the foundational Ohio holding that permanent custody requires a specific, enumerated statutory finding proved by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.quote: permanent custody may not be granted unless the trial court finds clear and convincing evidence that one or more of the eight enumerated factors in R.C. 2151.414(E) exist

key_cases.holding: The Court reversed a termination of parental rights that rested solely on the parents' cognitive disability, holding that a child's best interest may not be determined solely on the basis of the parents' limited cognitive abilities.
key_cases.relevance: It constrains the R.C. 2151.414 best-interest analysis by forbidding termination grounded solely on a parent's cognitive limitations.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the termination of appellants' parental rights based solely on mental retardation does not comply with R.C. 2151.414.

key_cases.holding: R.C. 2151.414(D)(1) requires a juvenile court to consider each listed best-interest factor but not to discuss each one expressly, so long as the reviewing court can discern from the decision and judgment entry that the factors were considered.
key_cases.relevance: It is the governing Ohio statement of how the R.C. 2151.414(D)(1) best-interest analysis must be documented at termination.
key_cases.quote: we hold that R.C. 2151.414(D)(1) does not require a juvenile court to expressly discuss each of the best-interest factors in R.C. 2151.414(D)(1)(a) through (e). Consideration is all the statute requires.

key_cases.holding: De minimis monetary gifts from a biological parent to a child are not maintenance and support under R.C. 3107.07(A), and the petitioner bears the burden of proving the failure to support and its lack of justifiable cause by clear and convincing evidence, with a dual standard of appellate review.
key_cases.relevance: Where adoption proceeds without parental consent, this case sets the burden of proof and the standard of review that decide whether the parent's veto survives.
key_cases.quote: A probate court determination of whether a financial contribution constitutes maintenance and support for purposes of R.C. 3107.07(A) is reviewed for an abuse of discretion

key_cases.holding: Denial of an indigent parent's request for appointed counsel in a probate adoption proceeding is a final, appealable order, and equal protection is violated by giving indigent parents appointed counsel when their rights are terminated in juvenile court but not when they are terminated by adoption in probate court.
key_cases.relevance: It extends appointed counsel to indigent parents contesting a stepparent or private adoption that would terminate their rights.
key_cases.quote: the child and the child's parents are statutorily entitled to legal representation, including a right to appointed counsel if they are indigent, at all stages of the proceedings

timeline_requirements.deadline: 12 months, then a review hearing at least every 12 months
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Earlier of the date the complaint was filed or the child was first placed in shelter care

timeline_requirements.deadline: 12 of 22 months (Ohio trigger, earlier than the federal 15 of 22)
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Child enters agency temporary custody — the earlier of adjudication under Ohio Rev. Code § 2151.28 or 60 days after removal from home
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not stated in the statute; the agency with custody must file the permanent custody motion unless an exception in Ohio Rev. Code § 2151.413(D)(3) applies
